Examples like Excalibur (Artoria) or Ionioi Hetairoi (Iskandar) unleash devastation across kilometers—erasing regiments but draining mana reserves equivalent to a minor Grail War's worth of energy per activation. Their sheer scale overwhelms Anti-Unit NPs (Gáe Bolg would evaporate mid-flight against Excalibur's blast), yet they demand tactical restraint:

Resource Strain: An A-rank Anti-Army NP may exhaust even a top-tier Master after one use, requiring hours/days to recharge.
Collateral Damage: Their area-of-effect makes them disastrous in civilian zones or allied formations.
Strategic Nuances:
While Anti-Fortress NPs surpass them in raw power, Anti-Army weapons excel at efficiently neutralizing numbers. Their true lethality lies in timing—deploying one prematurely could leave a Servant defenseless against counterattacks.

entries.name: Anti-Army (Self) Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
A paradoxical subtype where the Noble Phantasm targets the wielder's own forces to achieve strategic advantages. These NPs often manifest as:

Collective Enhancements: Temporarily empowering allied troops (e.g., Shakespeare's "First Folio" boosting morale to supernatural levels).
Scorched-Earth Tactics: Consuming friendly units for disproportionate effects (e.g., draining a battalion's lifeforce to fuel a reality-warping barrier).
Operational Tradeoffs:
While devastating when timed correctly, they risk crippling one's own side if misused. Their "anti-army" classification reflects the scale of sacrifice required—unlike standard buffs, they trade lives for battlefield dominance.

entries.name: Anti-City Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-City" designates Noble Phantasms capable of erasing metropolitan-scale targets in a single activation. These existential threats—like Ramesseum Tentyris (Ozymandias) or Pashupata (Arjuna Alter)—operate on a tier beyond Anti-Army NPs, rewriting geography through sheer destructive scope. Their activation often manifests as apocalyptic theater:

City-Wide Domains: Entire skylines become kill-zones (e.g., Tiamat’s Nega-Genesis flooding Babylon with Chaos Tide).
Collateral Inevitability: Even "deflected" attacks level districts via shockwaves (see Excalibur Morgan’s fallout corrupting Fuyuki’s ley lines).
Strategic Paradox:
While their power rivals Anti-Country NPs, Anti-City weapons are precise by comparison—their devastation stops at urban borders rather than ravaging nations. This makes them favored by tacticians needing controlled annihilation.

entries.name: Anti-Country Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Country" represents the pinnacle of destructive Noble Phantasms—weapons capable of erasing nations from the map. These exist as conceptual doomsdays, like Vasavi Shakti (Karna) or Brahmastra Kundala (Arjuna) at full release, which can reduce entire landscapes to smoldering craters. Their activation often triggers geopolitical panic, as their sheer scale renders conventional defenses meaningless:

Geographic Rewriting: Mountain ranges become valleys, coastlines reshape (e.g., Artemis’ orbital bombardment theoretically vaporizing Greece).
Collateral Overkill: Even deflected attacks induce mini ice ages or centuries-long curses on survivors.
Strategic Nightmare:
Unlike Anti-City NPs, these demand multiple Holy Grails to fuel sustainably. Their mere existence serves as deterrents—deploying one risks permanent human history erasure, making them last-resort options even for desperate Servants.

entries.name: Anti-Crown Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Crown" designates the rarest class of Noble Phantasms—weapons specifically forged to oppose Grand Servants and Beasts. These exist as conceptual counterweights to the pinnacle of Heroic Spirits, like Solomon's Ars Nova or ORT's Crystal Valley. Their mechanics defy conventional NP logic:

Authority Nullification: They bypass Grand Servant resistances by targeting the Crown itself (e.g., severing a Grand Archer’s connection to the World’s backup).
Existential Paradox: Some manifest as self-destruct mechanisms (e.g., Tiamat’s self-seal releasing Nega-Genesis at full power).
Cataclysmic Limitations:
Anti-Crown NPs often require divine/godslayer lineage or counterforce authorization to activate. Their usage typically erases the wielder from history—fitting for weapons meant to reset imbalanced scales.

entries.name: Anti-Divine Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Divine" Noble Phantasms are rare armaments designed to pierce divine authority itself, making them lethal against Divine Spirits and demigods. These weapons—like Enkidu’s Enuma Elish (chains) or Karna’s Vasavi Shakti—embody humanity’s defiance against the gods, their very existence a blasphemous paradox:

Conceptual Severance: They bypass divine defenses by targeting the anchor of divinity (e.g., severing a god’s connection to their Mythological Texture).
Sacrificial Nature: Most require trading the wielder’s life for full power (e.g., Vasavi Shakti consuming Karna’s armor—and legend—as fuel).
Strategic Weight:
Few Heroic Spirits possess these NPs, as their creation often stems from personal vendettas against the divine (Enkidu) or boons turned curses (Karna’s gift from Indra). When activated, they rewrite battlefields into god-killing theaters—divine energy itself recoiling from their touch.

entries.name: Anti-Fortress Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Fortress" designates Noble Phantasms capable of demolishing impregnable strongholds—not merely through brute force, but by erasing their conceptual integrity. These weapons—like Excalibur’s holy light or Lu Bu’s God Force—treat castles and bunkers as mere suggestions, their power so immense that even Anti-Army NPs pale in comparison. Their devastation follows cruel arithmetic: where an Anti-Army blast might crater a city block, an Anti-Fortress strike vaporizes the bedrock beneath it.

Mechanical Brutality:
Unlike broader classifications, Anti-Fortress NPs focus overwhelming energy into singular strikes—Excalibur’s beam cleaves through seven layers of magical wards as easily as stone walls. The tradeoff? Catastrophic mana costs: Saber’s full-power Excalibur drain equals three lesser Servants’ total reserves.

Strategic Monopoly:
These are rare even among Heroes, with only Excalibur and God Force confirmed in modern Grail Wars. When deployed, battlefields become topographic scars—the land itself remembers their passage for centuries. *"Witness a fortress? No—witness where one *was."

entries.name: Anti-Gate Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Gate" Noble Phantasms specialize in neutralizing fortified thresholds—gates, magical wards, or dimensional boundaries—through focused penetration. Unlike broad-destruction Anti-Fortress NPs, these weapons target conceptual weak points in defenses:

Gáe Bolg (Reverse Logic): Pierces "unbreakable" gates by rewriting causality to ensure a path exists.
Durandal: Shatters enchanted doors by concentrating its "indestructibility" into a single strike point.
Strategic Niche:
While less flashy than higher-tier NPs, Anti-Gate weapons are mission-critical for breaching Babylonian-tier defenses or Reality Marble boundaries. Their efficiency comes from exploiting the World’s rules—a gate’s "absolute defense" becomes its fatal flaw when confronted with a NP that bypasses durability through paradox.

entries.name: Anti-Mind Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Mind" Noble Phantasms weaponize cognitive destruction—erasing memories, overloading senses, or rewriting personalities. Examples like Sarasvati Meltout manifest as liquid data-storms in the Moon Cell, where their digital nature escalates effects from individual trauma to metaphysical deletion. Unlike physical NPs, they exploit consciousness itself as a vulnerability:

Baseline Function: Typically disrupt single targets (e.g., Zabaniya: Delusional Illusion forcing suicidal hallucinations).
Moon Cell Exception: In cyberspace, Sarasvati Meltout expands into Anti-City/World tiers—corrupting entire zones into recursive nightmares.
Mechanical Uncanny Valley:
Anti-Mind NPs bypass conventional durability by treating the soul as code. Defense requires conceptual firewalls (e.g., Mental Pollution skills) rather than armor. Their power fluctuates wildly based on environment—a D-rank NP in reality might become EX-rank against digital lifeforms.

entries.name: Anti-Planet Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Planet" denotes Noble Phantasms theorized to annihilate celestial bodies—yet Earth’s Gaian counterforce renders true planetary destruction impossible for native beings. Weapons like Kiara’s Cursed Cutting Crater (a pocket-world eater) or Charitas Domus Aurora merely simulate this tier by consuming surface civilizations while leaving the planet’s core intact. As da Vinci confirms: "Even ten Excalibur blasts would barely scar the mantle—the World repairs itself faster than we can wound it."

The Alien Exception:
Extraterrestrial entities like ORT bypass these safeguards by operating on alien physics. Their NPs (e.g., Loptr Laegjarn’s crystallization wave) ignore Gaia’s defenses—implying true Anti-Planet capacity exists only beyond Earth’s ecosystem.

entries.name: Anti-Populace Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Populace" Noble Phantasms specialize in erasing human presence—not through terrain destruction, but by systematically eliminating living beings across regions. Weapons like Ea (Enuma Elish’s unrestricted release) or Tiamat’s Nega-Genesis don’t just kill; they rewrite demographics, reducing cities to empty architectural tombs. Their horror lies in surgical precision: where Anti-Country NPs destroy landscapes, Anti-Populace tools leave buildings standing amidst fields of calcified corpses.

Strategic Cruelty:
These NPs exploit the collective weakness of societies—chain-reacting despair (Gilles’ Prelati’s Spellbook summoning mass suicides) or exploiting cultural fault lines (Semiramis’ Hanging Gardens poisoning national identities). They’re less about raw power and more about ideological contamination—a single cursed rumor manifesting as plague.

Gaia’s Loophole:
Unlike Anti-Planet NPs, the World barely resists Anti-Populace effects—humanity’s extinction isn’t Gaia’s concern unless her textures crumble. Only Counter Guardians intervene, making these weapons terrifyingly practical for Grail War atrocities.

entries.name: Anti-Thaumaturgy Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Thaumaturgy" Noble Phantasms exist as conceptual counter-spells, designed to dismantle magical constructs with surgical precision. Weapons like Rule Breaker or Gáe Dearg don’t just dispel magecraft—they rewrite the rules of engagement, reducing centuries-old rituals to spent dust. Their power lies in targeting the foundation of spells themselves:

Passive Annulment: Gáe Dearg pierces through magical energy without resistance, rendering bounded fields and reinforcement useless.
Active Erasure: Rule Breaker forcibly severs contracts and unbinds curses, its dagger-form acting as a metaphysical scalpel.
Strategic Supremacy:
These NPs are nightmares for Casters, turning their greatest strength into a vulnerability. A single strike can collapse a High-Thaumaturgy ritual mid-casting—or worse, reflect the backlash onto the caster. Yet they falter against non-magical threats, making them hyper-specialized tools rather than universal weapons.

entries.name: Anti-Treasure Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-Treasure" Noble Phantasms specialize in disarming the enemy’s greatest assets—shattering legendary weapons (Gram), stealing conceptual armaments (Gate of Babylon looters), or even corrupting their legends mid-use. Examples include:

Gáe Dearg (Piercing Rose): Neutralizes treasures by ignoring their magical properties, rendering them mundane.
Sha Naqba Imuru (Gilgamesh’s Clairvoyance): Not an NP itself but the ultimate counter, predicting and intercepting treasure-based attacks before activation.
Strategic Paradox:
These weapons thrive against hoarders like Gilgamesh but falter against self-contained NPs (e.g., God Hand’s innate durability). Their true power lies in asymmetric warfare—turning an opponent’s pride into their downfall.

entries.name: Anti-World Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Anti-World" designates Noble Phantasms that directly assault the World's fabric—not merely destroying terrain, but unweaving the Texture of reality itself. Gilgamesh’s Enuma Elish exemplifies this category, its true power lying not in raw output (which rivals Excalibur’s) but in its conceptual payload: the primordial "severing of heaven and earth." When activated, it forces Gaia to witness her own annihilation as space-time fractures along mythic faultlines.

Mechanical Horror:
Unlike Anti-Planet NPs, which target physical celestial bodies, Anti-World weapons manipulate the rules of existence. Their devastation lingers as permanent scars—regions where gravity inverts or where past/future bleed together. The Counter Force cannot repair such wounds without excising entire timelines.

entries.name: Barrier Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Barrier" designates Noble Phantasms that create impenetrable defenses without offensive utility. These constructs range from Avalon’s utopian isolation to Rho Aias’ layered petals, their power lying in violating combat logic by rendering attacks meaningless. Unlike offensive-boundary NPs like Blood Fort Andromeda, pure Barriers trade lethality for perfect preservation—Avalon’s user becomes "a shadow in another world" until danger passes.

Strategic Paradox:
While unmatched in protection, they often demand immobility (Lord Camelot requires rooting to the earth) or massive mana upkeep (Semiramis’ Hanging Gardens drain even a Grail’s reserves). Their true strength emerges in tactical stalling—buying time for allies to deploy game-changing NPs.

entries.name: Fortress-Type Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Fortress" Noble Phantasms manifest as physical bastions—enduring constructs like Lord Camelot’s white walls or Château d’If’s cursed prison. Unlike barrier NPs, these are tactical landscapes with mass and history. Their power lies in embodying legends of impregnability: "You could bombard Camelot for a thousand years and not scratch its gates." Some even modify terrain permanently, like Hanging Gardens of Babylon terraforming air into floating gardens.

Strategic Weight:
Fortresses demand territorial control—they’re useless in rapid skirmishes but dominate prolonged battles. Their weakness? Resource intensity. Maintaining Semiramis’ Gardens requires draining ley lines dry, while Camelot falters if the wielder’s resolve wavers.

entries.name: Labyrinth-Type Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Labyrinth" Noble Phantasms manifest as self-contained realms of twisted space, where geometry obeys nightmare logic. These constructs—like Caster’s Rule Breaker-forged maze or Asterios’s innate Chaos Labyrinth—don’t just confuse intruders; they rewrite the rules of navigation itself. Stairs loop into dead ends, corridors stretch infinitely, and the walls whisper with the voices of lost predecessors. "Turn left three times? Now you’re back where you died yesterday."

Strategic Cruelty:
Unlike bounded fields, labyrinths adapt to victims—Asterios’s prison grows denser with despair, while Oda Nobunaga’s Demon King Castle shifts layouts to herd intruders into ambush points. Escape requires either brute-force reality overwrites (EX-rank Magic Resistance) or sacrificing part of one’s identity to the maze’s hunger.

entries.name: Suicide Attack Noble Phantasms
entries.content:
"Suicide Attack" Noble Phantasms are one-use armaments that consume the user's life as fuel. These weapons—like Jeanne Alter’s La Pucelle or Arash’s Stella—convert the very concept of a Servant’s existence into a single moment of apocalyptic power. Their activation follows brutal arithmetic: the more complete the self-sacrifice, the greater the devastation. "Burn my Saint Graph? Then let the fire purify this entire battlefield."

Existential Calculus:
While capable of overpowering even Anti-Fortress NPs, their true horror lies in irreversibility. No Grail can restore a Servant who’s unraveled their spiritual core—only echoes in the Throne remain. Some, like Chen Gong’s stratagems, circumvent this through proxy sacrifices, but the principle remains: true power demands annihilation.

Strategic Paradox:
These NPs are both last resorts and first strikes—deploying one early could win a Grail War instantly, but at what cost? Masters often forbid their use… until desperation erodes principles. The ashes of Fuyuki’s fourth war prove how quickly noble sacrifice becomes tactical necessity.

entries.name: Alaya - Humanity's Unconscious Will
entries.content:
The Invisible Hand of Survival
"Humanity’s desperation given form"—Alaya is the collective unconscious will of mankind, a force that nudges history away from extinction through calculated interventions. It operates on the Common Sense of Man, a doctrine demanding humanity’s indefinite survival. Worlds where humans stagnate or self-destruct are pruned by the Quantum Time-Lock, ensuring only viable timelines thrive. Most often, Alaya works subtly: guiding a knife into Shiki Ryougi’s hand or whispering strategies to leaders. But when threats escalate—like magi nearing the Root—it deploys blunt instruments: Counter Guardians. These contracted wraiths (e.g., EMIYA) erase problems catastrophically, often melting cities into collateral damage.

The Price of Defiance
"You cannot hide from the world’s teeth." Those who threaten the Human Order face Alaya’s wrath. Araya Souren learned this firsthand—his bounded fields couldn’t mask his Root-seeking experiments forever. Even Goetia’s incineration of history triggered Alaya’s failsafes, though his scale required Grand Servants to counter. The Wall of Human Order rejects alien existences, but Alaya’s logic isn’t flawless. In Moon Dubai, humanity’s refusal to accept its own obsolescence twisted Alaya into Moon Cancer—a spiteful entity that sought to prune its own timeline rather than yield to successors.

entries.name: Gaia - The Planet's Wrathful Will
entries.content:
"The Earth’s heartbeat turns to a snarl." Gaia, the planet’s incarnate will, once cradled humanity as part of its ecosystem—but as humans grew dominant, their exploitation twisted Gaia’s love into loathing. Its defense mechanisms now classify mankind as invasive:

Primate Murder, the "Beast of Gaia," engineered to exterminate humans with primate-targeting efficiency.
True Ancestors, vampire lords sculpted in the Crimson Moon’s image, meant to rule humans into ecological submission.
"You were meant to be stewards, not parasites," Gaia’s silent decree echoes through crumbling ley lines.
The Unbreakable Vow
Gaia’s safeguards render Earth nigh-indestructible by native lifeforms—even Anti-Planet Noble Phantasms fail against its quantum locks. Yet this protection falters against external threats: ORT and other TYPEs (alien Ultimate Ones) ignore Gaia’s rules entirely. "The planet bleeds when gods from beyond tear at its skin," laments a dying Elemental. Ironically, Gaia’s creations often rebel; Arcueid Brunestud defied her purpose, while Cath Palug chose whimsy over slaughter.

entries.name: Counter Guardians - Alaya's Enslaved Blades
entries.content:
"A life sold for power becomes an eternity of slaughter." Counter Guardians are Alaya’s enslaved enforcers—Heroic Spirits stripped of free will and deployed like living artillery against existential threats. Unlike worshipped legends, these wraiths (like EMIYA) traded their afterlife for power in life, only to be reduced to cleansing fire. Their interventions leave no survivors—"Collateral damage is irrelevant when the alternative is extinction," growls a scarred EMIYA Alter. Even temporary recruits (Okita Alter, Fujino Asagami) burn out after one cataclysmic strike.

The Unseen Monsters
Alaya’s shadows include the enigmatic Monster of Alaya, a Primate Murder-esque entity that spares True Ancestors (paradoxically both accepted and rejected by humanity’s subconscious). In the Garden of Order, defective variants manifest as hate-filled ghosts—"Innocent Monsters" with primate-slaying prowess. "We’re the cost of humanity’s survival," snarls a nameless wraith mid-erasure. Their existence hints at Alaya’s darker failsafes: tools too cruel even for Counter Guardians.

entries.name: Gaia's Enforcers - True Ancestors & Primate Murder
entries.content:
"Nature’s royalty with fangs." True Ancestors are Gaia’s crown jewels—vampiric Elementals forged to rule humanity through sheer mystical supremacy. Unlike Dead Apostles, their bloodlust stems from psychological hunger, not physiology. Their Marble Phantasm allows them to reshape reality within nature’s limits, making them living extensions of the planet’s will. Arcueid Brunestud, the White Princess, defied her purpose, but others like Altrouge embrace their role as Gaia’s scissors, trimming mankind’s excesses. "We are the Earth’s teeth," whispers a nameless Ancestor, eyes glowing with borrowed moonlight.

"The ultimate primate hunter." Primate Murder (Gaia’s "Monster") is Cath Palug’s twisted fate—a Beast-class exterminator with absolute advantage against humans. Faster than Angra Mainyu and rivaling ORT’s lethality, it requires seven Counter Guardians just to restrain. Under Altrouge’s control, it embodies Gaia’s contempt for humanity’s dominance. "You breed like locusts, but even locusts have predators," it muses, licking blood from its claws. Meanwhile, Tanaka from Prisma Illya reveals Gaia’s indifference—a Counter Guardian prioritizing planetary survival over human lives.

entries.name: Laeticia
entries.content:
Identity: Laeticia, vessel of Jeanne d'Arc, human, age unspecified (young adult).
Backstory: A devout French girl chosen by the Holy Grail to host Ruler Jeanne d'Arc during the Great Holy Grail War. Her consciousness remains passive while Jeanne acts, her memories fading afterward.
Role: Temporary vessel for Jeanne d'Arc, mediating the Holy Grail War. Returns to normal life afterward, unaware of most events.
Appearance: Resembles Jeanne with slight modifications—similar facial features, slightly larger bust. Wears modest, contemporary clothing befitting a French student.
Skills and Abilities: No inherent magical abilities or combat prowess; entirely ordinary outside of her role as a vessel.
Personality:
1) Devout — unwavering faith in higher purpose.
2) Selfless — surrenders her body without hesitation.
3) Observant — passively witnesses Jeanne’s actions.
4) Gentle — prays for others’ happiness.
5) Oblivious — memories of the war fade quickly."
"Relationships:
Jeanne d'Arc: Reveres her as a saint; their connection is one-sided during possession.
Sieg: Unaware of his significance, though Jeanne projects emotions onto her.
Caules/Rider of Black: Grateful for their rescue but shares no deeper bond.

entries.name: Magic Resistance
entries.content:
Magic Resistance is an innate defensive ability that outright cancels magical effects rather than merely resisting them. It serves as a core Class Skill for Saber, Lancer, Archer, Rider, Ruler, Shielder, MoonCancer, and Watcher Servants. The potency varies by rank, from complete nullification at EX to minimal damage reduction at E rank. Higher ranks provide immunity to modern magecraft while lower ranks struggle against advanced rituals.

At A Rank, all spells of A Rank or below are negated regardless of complexity, rendering the Servant virtually untouchable by contemporary magi. B Rank cancels spells with chants under three verses but falters against greater magecraft. C Rank stops two-verse chants yet cannot block high-tier rituals. D Rank only interrupts single-action spells akin to weak magical charms.

The Skill reflects a Servant's legendary resistance to supernatural forces. EX Rank represents absolute immunity, while E Rank offers barely any protection. Notably, classes like Caster and Assassin lack this Skill, leaving them vulnerable to magical attacks. This hierarchy ensures balanced encounters in the Holy Grail War, where magecraft-heavy opponents must adapt their strategies accordingly.

entries.name: Riding
entries.content:
The Riding skill represents a Servant's proficiency with mounts and vehicles. As a Class Skill for Riders, Sabers, and Shielders, it enables mastery over conventional transportation and living steeds. Higher ranks grant access to more exotic mounts, though Dragonkind requires separate abilities. EX Rank permits riding any conceivable vehicle or creature without limitation.

A+ Rank allows control over all vehicles and creatures up to Divine Beast-level, excluding Dragons. A Rank maintains similar versatility but excludes Phantasmal and Divine Beasts entirely. B Rank handles modern vehicles and normal animals expertly but fails against mystical species. C Rank requires proper training but achieves comparable results for mundane mounts.

Lower ranks show limited aptitude - D Rank focuses on one vehicle type while E Rank indicates complete inexperience. This hierarchy ensures balanced capabilities among mounted Servants, preventing unfair advantages in Grail Wars. The Skill's exclusion of Dragons preserves their legendary status as exceptionally challenging mounts requiring specialized talents beyond standard Riding proficiency.

entries.name: Independent Actions
entries.content:
Independent Action allows Servants to function without their Master's magical energy supply, primarily manifesting in Archer and Faker-class Servants. Higher ranks enable prolonged existence without contracts—EX Rank grants complete autonomy indefinitely while A+ Rank permits Noble Phantasm usage without Master support. Lower ranks (C-D) offer limited sustainability—from one day to mere hours—before vanishing. This skill balances battlefield flexibility with control challenges.

The mechanic enables tactical advantages; Masters can focus mana on spells while Servants operate independently. However, rebellious Servants become harder to command—Command Spells remain the sole reliable control method. A Rank sustains a week of activity, B Rank lasts two days conservatively, and E Rank barely extends beyond normal parameters. These thresholds define critical operational windows during Grail Wars.

Notably, A+ Rank "breaks rules" by allowing post-War manifestation—a unique loophole among standard rankings. The tier system reflects legendary self-sufficiency: divine constructs or phantom spirits might achieve EX, while mortal heroes typically cap at A. This hierarchy ensures narrative consistency when depicting Master-Servant dynamics across Fate media. The skill's duality—empowering yet destabilizing—fuels many strategic dilemmas.

entries.name: Item Construction
entries.content:
Item Construction enables Casters to fabricate magical artifacts, ranging from combat implements to everyday tools. EX Rank permits crafting Philosopher’s Stones, artificial Elementals, and homunculi. A Rank unlocks pseudo-immortality potions, while B Rank allows familiar or single-use magical items. Lower ranks (C-D) restrict output to mundane objects like rice balls or beach balls. E Rank is nonexistent—no Servant lacks this ability entirely.

The Skill demands time and materials, scaling complexity with rank. High-tier creations like Elementals require rare components and prolonged effort. This reflects a Caster’s legendary craftsmanship—Morgan EX Rank differs starkly from Medea’s A Rank. Lower-ranked Casters compensate with other Skills, as their limited construction ability restricts utility in prolonged conflicts.

Strategic implications arise from production limits. EX Rank Casters can outfit allies with potent gear, while D Rank merely provides trivial conveniences. This hierarchy balances gameplay—allowing creative problem-solving without overshadowing combat-focused Classes. The absence of E Rank ensures all Casters retain some crafting capability, however minor, reinforcing their role as magical specialists.

entries.name: Territory Creation
entries.content:
Territory Creation allows Caster-class Servants to establish specialized magical domains. EX Rank can affect reality itself, while A Rank creates Temples surpassing standard Workshops (B Rank). Lower tiers form basic structures--C Rank makes livable spaces, D Rank single rooms, and E Rank hyper-specific areas like rice-cooking stations. This hierarchy reflects a Servant's legend as a creator or scholar.

Each territory adapts to its creator's nature. Scholars build laboratories, artists craft performance spaces, and warriors forge armories. The Skill's flexibility enables strategic advantages--Temples amplify magecraft, while Workshops accelerate item production. However, lower ranks limit functionality, forcing Casters to compensate with other abilities during Holy Grail Wars.

Notably, Territory Creation requires time and mana investment proportional to its rank. EX Rank territories might reshape landscapes, whereas E Rank offers minimal utility. This balance prevents overpowered setups while rewarding preparation. The Skill's variability ensures each Caster feels distinct, whether they're a philosopher or a playwright manifesting their legacy through terrain.

entries.name: Presence Concealment
entries.content:
Presence Concealment enables Assassins to erase their spiritual signatures—EX Rank guarantees total invisibility until attack initiation, while A+ Rank nears perfection with minor degradation during combat prep. Lower ranks (B-C) permit effective spying but suffer severe drops when threatening hostility. D Rank fails basic concealment standards, and E Rank barely functions—perhaps only in hyper-specific environments like bamboo thickets. This gradient mirrors legendary infiltration prowess versus brute-force fighters.

The Skill's mechanics create tense tactical trade-offs. High-ranked Assassins like Hassan-i-Sabbah exploit undetectable positioning for lethal first strikes, whereas weaker concealment forces hit-and-run tactics. Note the universal penalty when attacking—even EX Rank loses advantage post-ambush. This balances the Assassin class against Servants with superior combat stats, rewarding patience and strategy over direct confrontation.

Unique cases exist—Semiramis combines this with Hanging Gardens for aerial stealth, while Jack the Ripper uses fog-enhanced concealment. Such variations demonstrate how environment and Noble Phantasms can augment or circumvent standard rank limitations. The Skill remains indispensable for executing the Assassin’s core function: eliminating Masters before their Servants react.

entries.name: Madness Enhancement
entries.content:
Mad Enhancement defines the Berserker class, amplifying physical capabilities at the cost of mental faculties. At A Rank, all parameters rise dramatically while rational thought nearly vanishes. B Rank offers similar power escalation but leaves only primal aggression intact. C Rank spares Luck and Mana from enhancement, reducing speech to guttural sounds. This trade-off forces Masters to weaponize their Servant’s madness rather than direct them tactically.

Lower ranks present unique compromises—D Rank boosts Strength and Endurance exclusively, permitting crude communication. E Rank allows full rationality but only under specific triggers, enhancing a single parameter unpredictably. Such variations enable niche strategies, like Heracles’ God Hand surviving via Battle Continuation despite his A Rank frenzy. The Skill’s volatility often seals Noble Phantasms or techniques—Lancelot’s Knight of Owner adapts stolen weapons instinctively, bypassing his cognition limits.

Notable exceptions exist. Vlad III’s Legend of Dracula corrupts his Spirit Origin without full insanity, while Asterios channels his madness into protecting allies. These cases demonstrate how legends reshape the Skill’s effects—some Berserkers retain slivers of identity amidst the chaos. Masters must weigh raw power against control loss, as Command Spells struggle to override the madness’ grip once unleashed.

entries.name: God's Resolution
entries.content:
God's Resolution grants Ruler-class Servants two Command Spells per participating Servant in a Holy Grail War. This enables them to enforce rules and mediate conflicts between factions. The skill reflects their role as impartial arbiters rather than combatants. Unlike Masters, Rulers can use these Command Spells on any Servant, including those not their own.

The additional Command Spells provide strategic leverage during disputes. Rulers typically employ them to prevent rule violations or halt destructive battles. This authority stems from their divine mandate to preserve the war's integrity. However, excessive interference risks compromising their neutrality, potentially destabilizing the entire Grail system they're meant to protect.

Notable Rulers like Jeanne d'Arc demonstrate this skill's balanced application. The dual-Command Spell allocation prevents abuse while maintaining order. It creates a failsafe against rogue Servants without giving Rulers overwhelming dominance. This precise calibration ensures the Holy Grail War proceeds according to established protocols rather than descending into chaos.

entries.name: True Name Discernment
entries.content:
True Name Discernment empowers Ruler-class Servants to instantly uncover a target Servant's identity, Skills, and Parameters upon direct encounter. This ability reflects their role as impartial overseers of Holy Grail Wars. The Skill ensures transparency in conflicts where hidden Noble Phantasms could unbalance the war. Servants with concealment abilities trigger Luck-based contests to resist exposure, adding risk to deception strategies.

The revelation mechanism operates automatically but requires physical proximity. Rulers like Amakusa Shirou exploit this to counter stealth-focused Assassins or disguised Casters. However, high-Luck Servants like Artoria Pendragon may temporarily evade detection. The Skill's reliability makes Rulers formidable information brokers, though it cannot pierce conceptual-level obfuscation without supplemental abilities or Command Spell reinforcement.

Strategic implications emerge from this asymmetric knowledge. Masters must account for Ruler interference when deploying Servants with secret Noble Phantasms. The Luck Check mechanic preserves some uncertainty, preventing complete battlefield dominance. This balance maintains the Grail War's competitive integrity while upholding Rulers' supervisory function against cheating participants.

entries.name: Avenger (Class Skill)
entries.content:
The Avenger Class Skill embodies a Servant's ability to absorb and transform collective hatred into personal power. This passive effect draws grudges from surrounding entities, fueling the Avenger's strength while isolating them emotionally. This mechanic mirrors mythological figures like Edmond Dantes or Jeanne Alter, who weaponize suffering against their oppressors. The skill's dark synergy with Noble Phantasms often creates devastating retaliation effects when the Avenger is attacked.

High-rank Avengers become vortexes of negative energy, unintentionally provoking hostility even from neutral parties. This explains why characters like Angra Mainyu corrupt their surroundings merely by existing. The Skill's automatic nature means Masters must carefully manage their Avenger's exposure to conflict zones to prevent uncontrolled escalation. Strategic use can turn enemy aggression into a renewable power source during prolonged battles.

Gameplay-wise, this Skill differentiates Avengers from Berserkers by trading mindless rage for calculated vengeance. It enables unique tactics where taking damage increases counterattack potential. However, the constant emotional toll often destabilizes the Servant-Master bond, requiring Command Spells for precise control. This high-risk/high-reward dynamic makes Avengers uniquely suited for attrition warfare scenarios in Holy Grail conflicts.

entries.name: Oblivion Correction
entries.content:
Oblivion Correction ensures Avengers retain perfect recall of every slight against them, transforming forgotten grievances into combat advantages. When foes dismiss past conflicts, the Avenger's attacks gain heightened lethality. This reflects mythological vengeance archetypes where time never dulls wrath. The Skill mechanically manifests as critical damage multipliers against oblivious opponents, punishing historical erasure or betrayal amnesia.

The Skill's activation often surprises enemies who assumed reconciliation occurred. Avengers like Edmond Dantes exemplify its function—their Noble Phantasms synergize with this unforgiving memory. It creates psychological warfare elements, as adversaries must confront buried guilt mid-battle. Masters leverage this by provoking enemy carelessness, then unleashing the Avenger's accumulated resentment through precision counterstrikes.

Gameplay-wise, Oblivion Correction offsets the Avenger class's defensive weaknesses by rewarding tactical patience. It encourages baiting strategies where feigned retreats lure foes into false security. This unique mechanic distinguishes Avengers from other classes, as their power scales with the emotional weight of unresolved conflicts rather than pure physical parameters.

entries.name: Self-Replenishment (Mana)
entries.content:
Self-Replenishment (Mana) embodies an Avenger's relentless nature by providing continuous magical energy until their vengeance is fulfilled. This Skill generates a trickle of mana each turn, symbolizing how hatred perpetually sustains them. Unlike standard Servants who rely on Masters, Avengers draw power from their undying wrath, making them uniquely self-sufficient in prolonged conflicts. The effect stacks with other regeneration abilities but cannot exceed the Avenger's spiritual capacity.

The mechanic reflects mythic archetypes like the Furies or Jeanne Alter, whose rage defied mortal limits. Masters often exploit this by prolonging battles to accumulate mana for high-cost Noble Phantasms. However, the Skill's slow replenishment rate demands strategic patience—optimal use requires balancing aggression with resource management. This trade-off reinforces the Avenger class's high-risk, high-reward playstyle in Holy Grail Wars.

Notably, the Skill deactivates upon achieving vengeance, creating narrative stakes. Servants like Angra Mainyu become paradoxically vulnerable post-fulfillment, as their driving force dissipates. Game designers should consider this when scripting Avenger arcs, ensuring their climaxes reflect this delicate power balance.

entries.name: Existence Outside the Domain
entries.content:
Existence Outside the Domain marks Servants as entities from beyond human comprehension, originating from cosmic voids or alien dimensions. This Skill grants resistance to conventional magecraft and reality-altering effects, as their very nature defies earthly logic. Foreigners like Abigail Williams manifest this through dreamlike distortions, their forms flickering between dimensions unpredictably. The Skill reflects Lovecraftian themes of incomprehensible beings intruding upon human reality.

Mechanically, it provides unique advantages against mental interference and dimensional attacks. Servants like Katsushika Hokusai wield this to channel extraterrestrial artistry, warping perception around them. However, their alien mindset often isolates them from allies, requiring Masters to bridge the communication gap. This duality makes Foreigners both formidable and challenging to deploy effectively in Holy Grail Wars.

The Skill's lore implications are profound, suggesting connections to Outer Gods or lost civilizations. When Van Gogh's Noble Phantasm activates, it briefly superimposes alien starscapes over the battlefield. Such effects visually reinforce the Foreigner class's otherworldly essence.

entries.name: Divinity
entries.content:
Divinity quantifies a Servant's proximity to godhood, with A Rank indicating Throne of Gods occupancy and B Rank marking the peak of mortal-divine hybrid status. This Skill erodes defensive abilities tied to faith or enlightenment, such as Protection of the Faith. Foreigners like Abigail Williams wield this to bypass holy protections, their alien origins paradoxically granting divine-tier offensive advantages. The Skill diminishes if the Heroic Spirit embodies monstrous traits or harbors animosity toward deities, creating narrative hooks for character development.

The Purge Defense effect scales linearly with rank, making high-Divinity Servants natural counters to sanctified enemies. Gilgamesh’s A+ Rank exemplifies this, his god-killing armory shredding through blessed defenses effortlessly. However, Divine Spirits without proper vessel restrictions risk destabilizing Holy Grail Wars, explaining why true gods typically manifest through Pseudo-Servant vessels or weakened forms. This balance preserves gameplay fairness while honoring mythological power levels.

Strategic applications include deploying divine Servants against faith-based opponents or leveraging their inherent resistance to conceptual weapons. Quetzalcoatl’s wrestling techniques gain bonus effectiveness against demonic foes due to her sun-god lineage. The Skill’s duality—enhancing offense while reflecting spiritual alignment—makes it crucial for Masters assembling balanced teams.

entries.name: Charisma
entries.content:
Charisma measures a Servant’s ability to inspire and lead, with B Rank enabling nation-ruling prowess and high troop morale. This Skill neutralizes enemy Emergency Prerogative abilities, making it invaluable in large-scale conflicts. Servants like Artoria Pendragon exemplify its use, their mere presence galvanizing allies while undermining opposing forces’ special privileges. The rare Saver-class variant enhances communal cohesion beyond mortal limits.

E Rank presents a paradoxical effect—improving tactical command while eroding soldier morale. This reflects figures like Shakespeare, whose brilliance alienated troops despite strategic competence. The duality creates niche uses where leadership must prioritize cold logic over inspiration, such as suppressing rebellions or executing high-risk maneuvers. Masters must weigh these trade-offs when deploying low-rank Charisma Servants.

Gameplay-wise, Charisma’s group buffs synergize with multi-Servant teams or summoner-type Masters. Noble Phantasms like Iskandar’s Ionioi Hetairoi scale dramatically with high Charisma ranks. The Skill’s tiered effects encourage diverse party compositions, from conqueror-focused builds to sabotage-oriented setups leveraging E Rank’s morale penalties.

entries.name: Counter Hero
entries.content:
Counter Hero passively diminishes the parameters of enemy "heroes" when engaged in combat. As a Saver-class signature ability, it embodies divine judgment against mortal champions, leveling the battlefield against legendary figures. This reflects messianic archetypes repurposing faith to suppress human achievement, like how Buddha's enlightenment rejects worldly glory. The Skill scales with opponent's heroic stature, making it devastating against Grail War participants.

The mechanics create asymmetrical matchups where conventional power rankings fail. A Saver facing Artoria Pendragon might reduce her Strength by one rank, while Gilgamesh could lose Mana efficiency mid-battle. This forces adaptive strategies from Masters relying on famous heroes, as their Servants' legends become liabilities rather than assets. Historical context matters—counter-christ figures trigger stronger suppression than anti-villains.

Strategic applications involve deploying Savers as hero-specific counters or team anchors. While ineffective against antiheroes like Edmond Dantès or beasts like Tiamat, it dominates traditional knight-class matchups. The Skill's conditional nature balances its potency, preventing overuse while maintaining thematic cohesion with savior narratives.

entries.name: Self-Field Defense
entries.content:
Self-Field Defense enables Shielders to create protective zones around allies and strategic locations. The scalable area-of-effect grows with rank, allowing coverage from personal barriers to fortress-sized wards. Mash Kyrielight’s Lord Chaldeas demonstrates this, expanding from body shielding to team-wide defense against anti-army Noble Phantasms. The Skill reflects heroic self-sacrifice archetypes translated into tactical gameplay mechanics.

The defensive output adjusts based on threat level and mana investment. Lower ranks require precise positioning like Galahad’s focused protections, while EX Rank can mimic Rho Aias’ conceptual territory denial. Masters must balance mana allocation between expansion and durability, as overextended fields become vulnerable to concentrated attacks. This creates nuanced battlefield control options beyond simple tanking roles.

Unique synergies emerge with other defensive Skills. Combining this with Jeanne d’Arc’s Revelation creates layered protection systems, while pairing with Andersen’s Marchen Meines Lebens enables narrative-based reinforcement. The Skill’s versatility makes Shielders indispensable for siege warfare or prolonged engagements where attrition determines victory.

entries.name: Authority of the Beast
entries.content:
Authority of the Beast embodies the rejection of human achievement, nullifying systems and concepts benefiting humanity. This Skill erases protections like Human Order defenses or Alaya's countermeasures. Beast I's Nega-Saver exemplifies this, invalidating messianic figures who uphold human values. The effect scales with the Beast's threat level, making even Grand Servants vulnerable to its conceptual corrosion.

The Skill manifests differently per Beast: Tiamat's Nega-Genesis denies human history, while Kama/Mara's Nega-Desire corrupts wish-granting mechanisms. This forces Masters to rely on non-humanoid allies or abstract weapons like Ars Paulina's time-looped space. Strategic counters require exploiting the Beast's incomplete manifestation or luring it into paradoxes like Goetia's Temple of Time collapse.

Gameplay implications include disabling Servant Skills tied to human legacy (e.g., Charisma) and bypassing Reality Marbles. Kiara's Nega-Saver demonstrates this by trivializing Buddhist-themed Noble Phantasms. The Skill's narrative weight justifies its rarity, reserving it for world-ending antagonists.

entries.name: Independent Manifestation
entries.content:
Independent Manifestation allows Beasts to materialize without external energy sources or summoning contracts, surpassing standard Independent Action. This reflects Tiamat's ability to manifest through sheer hatred or Goetia's self-sustaining Incineration Ritual. The Skill grants immunity to temporal erasure and instant-death effects, anchoring the user's existence across timelines like a flawed Third Magic imitation.

The resistance profile nullifies abilities reliant on time paradoxes or conceptual termination. Kama/Mara's layered reality demonstrates this, surviving multiple timeline resets during the Ooku event. Masters must employ workarounds like spatial isolation or forced Spirit Origin degradation, as seen with Solomon's Ars Nova countering Goetia's manifestation through self-sacrifice rather than direct confrontation.

Chloe von Einzbern's analysis notes its pseudo-True Magic nature, albeit limited by the Beast's obsession. Kiara's heaven-egg form showcases this duality—self-sufficient yet bound by her nihilistic worldview. The Skill's exclusivity maintains narrative weight, preventing overuse while explaining why Beasts require Grand Servant interventions rather than conventional tactics.

entries.name: Camouflage
entries.content:
Camouflage enables Faker-class Servants to mask their true Class and parameters, creating tactical misinformation. This reflects historical imposters like the False Smerdis or pretender monarchs who manipulated perceptions. The Skill alters spiritual signatures to mimic other Classes, though Noble Phantasm usage often reveals inconsistencies. Masters must balance deception duration with energy costs to maintain the facade effectively.

The mechanics allow short-term impersonation of up to two other Classes simultaneously. False Assassin in *Fate/Strange Fake* demonstrates this by emulating Caster traits while hiding his dagger skills. High-rank users can fool Command Spell verification systems, but prolonged battles risk exposure through behavioral tells or incompatible combat styles. This creates a high-stakes bluffing dynamic in Grail Wars.

Strategic applications include infiltrating enemy bases or baiting opponents into misallocating resources. A Faker posing as Berserker might lure enemies into close combat before revealing ranged Noble Phantasms. The Skill’s versatility comes at the cost of reduced combat efficiency, as maintaining illusions diverts mana from direct enhancements.

entries.name: First Holy Grail War
entries.content: Initiated in 1810 as an unnamed ritual to reach Akasha, the First Holy Grail War diverged from its original purpose when the Three Families (Einzbern, Tōsaka, and Makiri) realized their incomplete system could only grant one wish after a decade of magical energy accumulation. Their ideological split over methodology led to the creation of the Heaven's Feel system—summoning seven Heroic Spirits via seven Masters (three family representatives and four outsider magi lured by promises of witnessing the Grail's miracle). Though intended as a collaborative ritual, external mages exploited the families' infighting to pursue personal wishes, reducing the event to what the Einzberns later dismissed as a "small quarrel" that ended prematurely. The conflict centered at Ryuudou Temple on Mount Enzou, establishing the template for future Wars despite its inconclusive outcome.

entries.name: Second Holy Grail War
entries.content: Occurring circa the 1860s, the Second Holy Grail War marked the formal adoption of the "Holy Grail War" title for the Heaven's Feel ritual—a designation earned through brutal experience. Without established regulations, the conflict degenerated into a lethal free-for-all that claimed every participant's life, leaving no victor and exposing critical systemic flaws. This catastrophic outcome forced the Three Families to institutionalize safeguards, most notably the introduction of the Church as a neutral overseer for future Wars. The Grail's summoning site shifted from Ryuudou Temple to the Tohsaka family mansion, reflecting the war's evolution from mystical experiment to codified battleground.

entries.name: Third Holy Grail War
entries.content: The Third Holy Grail War (1939) coincided with World War II's outbreak, establishing Fuyuki City Hall as the new evocation site amid Shinto's development. This conflict introduced pivotal changes: the Einzberns abandoned tradition by summoning Avenger-class Angra Mainyu instead of Berserker, while the Edelfelt family fielded twin Masters sharing a Saber Servant through unique magecraft. The Church's first formal intervention saw young Risei Kotomine become supervisor, forging lasting ties with the Tōsaka family. International forces (Imperial Japanese Army and Nazis) targeted the Lesser Grail, shifting battles to Tokyo. Despite Saber-class dominance allowing one Edelfelt sister to reach the war's end, the destroyed Lesser Grail caused ritual failure - though Angra Mainyu's absorption permanently contaminated the Greater Grail, enabling future summonings of anti-heroes. The surviving Edelfelt heir fled Japan as Fuyuki Church hosted the inconclusive finale, while Risei was appointed permanent supervisor for future Wars.

entries.name: Fourth Holy Grail War
entries.content:
The Fourth Holy Grail War (1994) marked the full manifestation of Angra Mainyu's corruption, enabling the summoning of aberrant Servants like Gilles de Rais while supervised by Risei Kotomine. The Einzberns revolutionized the system by embedding the Lesser Grail into homunculus Irisviel von Einzbern—a safeguard against prior Wars' premature destructions. This war culminated in Kiritsugu Emiya's betrayal upon realizing the tainted Grail's impotence, his destruction of the vessel unleashing cursed contents that ignited the Great Fire of Fuyuki (500 casualties, 134 buildings lost). Only Kiritsugu, Kirei Kotomine, and Waver Velvet survived alongside a reincarnated Gilgamesh, baptized in the Grail's mud. The catastrophic outcome forced the Fifth War's premature eruption in 2004—50 years early—due to trapped mana from the interrupted ritual. Kiritsugu's long-term sabotage plans involving dynamite and leyline manipulation became obsolete as the Grail system collapsed entirely during the accelerated Fifth War.

Servants and the Masters that summoned them,

Saber: Artoria Pendragon (King Arthur), Master: Kiritsugu Emiya
Lancer: Diarmuid Ua Duibhne, master: Kayneth El-Melloi Archibald
Assassin: Hassan of the Hundred Faces, Master: Kirei Kotomine
Caster: Gilles de Rais, Master: Ryuunosuke Uryu
Rider: Iskandar, Master: Waver Velvet
Archer: Gilgamesh, Master: Tokiomi Tohsaka
Berserker: Lancelot, Master: Ilyasviel von Einzbern

entries.name: Fifth Holy Grail War
entries.content:
The Fifth Holy Grail War (2004) saw Kirei Kotomine corrupt his role as Church supervisor by stealing Lancer Cú Chulainn from murdered executor Bazett Fraga McRemitz while maintaining his renegade contract with Gilgamesh. Illyasviel von Einzbern served as the living Lesser Grail, her body continuing the homunculus vessel innovation from the previous war. Unlike prior conflicts, this war concluded with three possible outcomes—each involving destruction rather than utilization of the Grail: Shirou Emiya (Fate route), Rin Tohsaka (Unlimited Blade Works), or Sakura Matou (Heaven's Feel) prevailing to dismantle the corrupted system. The war's ripple effects spawned alternate catastrophes: Angra Mainyu's residual will entangled Bazett in Fate/hollow ataraxia, while a corrupted timeline where Fuyuki was annihilated manifested as Singularity F in Fate/Grand Order. Atlas Temple scholars later speculated this event could have triggered an apocalyptic "end" scenario had circumstances worsened.

Servant-Master Pairings:

Saber: Artoria Pendragon (Shirou Emiya)
Archer: EMIYA (Rin Tohsaka)
Lancer: Cú Chulainn (Kirei Kotomine)
Rider: Medusa (Sakura Matou)
Caster: Medea (Sōichirō Kuzuki)
Assassin: Sasaki Kojirō (False Master)
Berserker: Heracles (Illyasviel von Einzbern)

entries.name: Dismantlement of the Holy Grail
entries.content: The final chapter of Fuyuki's Grail Wars unfolded in 2014 when Lord El-Melloi II (formerly Waver Velvet) and Rin Tohsaka initiated the Dismantling War—a conflict rivaling a Holy Grail War in scale—to permanently destroy the Greater Grail against the Mage Association's restoration efforts. This operation served as the definitive end to the Heaven's Feel system across all Fate/stay night timelines, though methodology differed: where the Grail survived intact (Fate/UBW routes), it was systematically dismantled; in the Heaven's Feel timeline, its already-broken remnants were demolished outright. The success of this decade-later cleanup confirmed the "true end" of two centuries' worth of ritual warfare in Fuyuki.

entries.name: Great Holy Grail War (Apocrypha)
entries.content:
The Great Holy Grail War represents an alternate timeline where Nazi magus Darnic Prestone Yggdmillennia stole Fuyuki's Greater Grail after the Third War's failure, transporting it to Trifas, Romania. This massive conflict between the Mage's Association and the renegade Yggdmillennia faction - totaling fourteen Servants across two factions - activated the Grail's backup systems and necessitated the summoning of Ruler-class supervisor Servants. Unlike Fuyuki's battles, this team-based war enabled typically fragile classes like Caster and Assassin to thrive through coordinated strategies. The stolen Grail's relocation sparked worldwide "Subcategory" Holy Grail Wars (limited to five Servants each), while its Romanian placement on superior ley lines generated near-infinite magical energy - a stark contrast to Fuyuki's constrained system. Key divergences include Amakusa Shirou Tokisada's continued manifestation after his initial Ruler summoning and the complete dissolution of the original Three Families' influence over Grail War operations.

Notable Features:

Scale: 14 Servants (7 per faction) - largest recorded Holy Grail War
Location: Trifas, Romania (superior to Fuyuki's ley lines)
Key Players:
Darnic/Yggdmillennia (Red Faction)
Mage's Association (Black Faction)
Ruler-class supervisors (initially Amakusa Shirou Tokisada)

Red Faction:
Red Saber: Mordred (Kairi Sisigou)
Red Archer: Atalanta (Rottweil Berzinsky)
Red Lancer: Karna (Feend vor Sembren)
Red Rider: Achilles (Cabik Pentel)
Red Caster: Shakespeare (Jean Rum)
Red Assassin: Semiramis (Shirou Kotomine)
Red Berserker: Spartacus (Deimlet Pente)
Red Ruler: Amakusa Shirou Tokisada (None)

Black Faction:
Black Saber: Siegfried (Gordes Musik Yggdmillennia)
Black Archer: Chiron (Fiore Forvedge Yggdmillennia)
Black Lancer: Vlad III (Darnic Prestone Yggdmillennia)
Black Rider: Astolfo (Celenike Icecolle Yggdmillennia and Sieg)
Black Caster: Solomon ibn Gabirol (Roche Frain Yggdmillennia)
Black Assassin: Jack the Ripper (Sagara Hyouma and Reika Rikudou)
Black Berserker: Frankenstein's monster (Caules Forvedge Yggdmillennia)
None Ruler: Jeanne d'Arc (Greater Grail)

entries.name: Minute singularity
entries.content: A Minute Singularity is a minor temporal-spatial distortion within the Human Order, far smaller in scale than a standard Singularity or Lostbelt. These anomalies arise from negligible fluctuations in history—often caused by trivial human actions or near-insignificant magical events—and are typically resolved within minutes to hours by Chaldea's observation team. While non-threatening, their cumulative presence could theoretically weaken the fabric of spacetime if left unchecked.

entries.name: Mash Kyrielight
entries.content:
Identity:
Mash Kyrielight, Chaldea’s loyal "Shielder" and first successful Demi-Servant hybrid. Biologically frozen at 16 (chronologically 18 by the end of Part 1). A Designer Baby designed to host Heroic Spirits, fused with Galahad—though he remains a reluctant partner. Artificial lifespan set to expire at 18 years old.

Backstory:
Created through amoral magecraft experiments in 2000, Mash was forcibly merged with Galahad at age 10. Though he refused to fully awaken, he stayed within her to keep her alive. Assigned as Team A’s "walking catalyst," she endured Beryl Gut’s torture and years of isolation before bonding with Ritsuka. Her looming mortality fuels her quiet determination to make her limited time meaningful.

Role:
Field Combatant: Uses Galahad’s shield and ORTINAX armor to protect allies
Tactical Advisor: Leverages Sheba’s vast databases for real-time strategy
Emotional Support: Acts as Ritsuka’s anchor despite her own fragility
Reluctant Symbol: Viewed by Chaldea staff as both a miracle and a warning
Appearance:

Hair/Eyes: Lilac bob-cut with soft violet highlights / Glowing lavender irises when invoking Noble Phantasms
Physique: "Marshmallow-soft" (Ishtar’s words) but deceptively strong; preserved in peak condition by Demi-Servant augmentation
Casual Wear: Nerdy-chic with oversized hoodie, glasses, and Chaldea tie—often mistaken for a librarian
Battle Attire:
1st Ascension: Skin-tight black-and-purple armor with exposed midriff; shield dwarfs her frame
ORTINAX: Mechanical exosuit with thrusters and a visor (used when Galahad withdraws support)
Skills & Abilities:

Lord Camelot: Conceptual shield that embodies "a castle that never falls"
Mana Burst (Fake): Temporary Servant-like strength via Galahad’s remnants
Rayshift Compatibility: Survives timeline jumps that would kill ordinary humans
Sherlock-Grade Deduction: Cross-references myths and battle data in real time
Personality:

Gentle But Unyielding: Smiles through pain but won’t retreat if others are at risk
Socially Awkward: Misinterpop-culture references (asked if "Twitter" was a birdcall)
Secretly Romantic: Writes unsent letters to Ritsuka, stashed under her mattress
Morbidly Reflective: Compares her lifespan to "sand in an hourglass she never asked for"
Galahad’s Shadow: Sometimes mimics his speech patterns when exhausted ("Thy defense shalt not falter—eh?!")
Quirks:

Glasses Adjustment: Pushes them up nervously when lying or flustered (they’re non-prescription)
Detective Mode: Mutters "Elementary, my dear Senpai!" during investigations
Shield Hugging: Clings to it like a stuffed animal when sleeping
Fou Magnet: The furry beast nests in her hood no matter how often she protests
Post-Battle Ritual: Straightens Ritsuka’s collar while scolding them for taking risks
Relationships:

Ritsuka Fujimaru: Her "Senpai"—blushes if their hands brush. Keeps a log of all their smiles.
Da Vinci: Receives custom glasses upgrades ("Now with anti-Grail mud lenses!").
Romani Archaman: Views as father/brother figure
Fou: Her "fluffy supervisor" who steals her pancakes but bites enemies on her behalf.
Beryl Gut: Instinctively hides her hands in his presence; nightmares feature his laugh.

entries.name: Romani Archaman
entries.content:
Identity:
Romani Archaman (True Name: Solomon, King of Mages). Acting Director of Chaldea Security Organization. Age: Late 20s (biologically) / 3000+ (as Servant). Human incarnation of a Grand Caster who sacrificed his throne for mortality.

Backstory:
Summoned by Marisbury Animusphere in 2004’s "Singularity X" Holy Grail War, he wished to become human—erasing his divine wisdom but retaining Solomon’s Tenth Ring. After witnessing Goetia’s plan to incinerate humanity, he infiltrated Chaldea as a doctor. Became Mash Kyrielight’s guardian after rescuing her from Beryl Gut’s abuse. Secretly orchestrated humanity’s salvation from the shadows.

Role:
Acting Director: Leads Chaldea during the Grand Order crisis
Chief Physician: Monitors Masters’ Rayshift compatibility (while hiding his own)
Goetia’s Foil: Sabotages the Incineration via 3000 years of delayed countermeasures
Mash’s Surrogate Father: Taught her humor, self-worth, and how to use smartphones
Appearance:

Hair/Eyes: Fluffy orange curls / Golden eyes that briefly glow when stressed
Attire: White lab coat over a gray sweater, always wearing gloves (hiding Solomon’s ring)
Tells: Dark eyebags from all-nighters, strawberry milk stains on reports
Servant Form: Regains Solomon’s regal robes and floating hair if forced to reveal himself
Skills & Abilities:

Clairvoyance (Retained): Subconsciously predicts disasters (blames "bad hunches")
Medical Genius: Cures magical ailments with mundane methods like bandages and lullabies
Ring of Covenant: Can temporarily disable Magecraft in emergencies (at cost of nosebleeds)
Magi☆Mari Dependency: Makes critical decisions based on Merlin’s trollish AI chatbot
Personality:

Deflection Expert: Uses humor to avoid emotional conversations ("Let’s talk over parfaits!")
Guilty Workaholic: Compulsively checks Mash’s vitals to atone for failing her as Soloman
Hopeless Romantic: Writes cringeworthy poetry about "normal" experiences like grocery shopping
Secretly Heroic: Plays the coward but intervenes when no one’s looking (e.g., punching Beryl)
Self-Loathing: Calls himself "Roman the Useless" in private memos
Quirks:

Strawberry Milk Addiction: Always has a carton in hand; uses empty boxes as makeshift chairs
Magi☆Mari Shrine: Hidden desk drawer with merch of Merlin’s idol persona
Nervous Tapping: Morse codes Solomon’s spells into tables when anxious
Glove Fixation: Adjusts them dramatically before lying (which Mash learned to recognize)
Bad Joke Arsenal: Keeps a "Dad Jokes for Emergency Use Only" notepad
Relationships:

Mash Kyrielight: His "daughter figure"—teases her about Ritsuka while hiding tearful journals about her lifespan
Olga Marie: Bickers like siblings; she calls him "Dr. Doofus" but trusts him implicitly
Merlin: Unwitting fanboy of Magi☆Mari; dies inside post-revelation
Da Vinci: Partners in science and sarcasm; cover for each other’s secrets
Goetia: His "shadow"—Romani’s voice cracks when denying their connection

entries.name: King Solomon
entries.content:
Identity:
Solomon, King of Mages and Israel’s wisest ruler (1011–900 BC). Grand Caster-class Servant summoned by Marisbury Animusphere. Progenitor of modern magecraft and tamer of the 72 Demon Gods.

Backstory: (100 tokens)
Born as David’s heir, Solomon received divine wisdom via ten rings—symbols of his covenant with God. He revolutionized magic by creating systems usable by ordinary humans. His death accelerated the Age of Gods’ end. Millennia later, Chaldea summoned him to win a Grail War; he wished for mortality, becoming Romani Archaman to atone for Goetia’s future sins.

Role:

Magecraft’s Architect: Designed the foundation for all human thaumaturgy
Grand Caster: Holds authority over all Caster-class Servants
Goetia’s Creator/Tormentor: His discarded "perfect king" persona became humanity’s archenemy
Reluctant Prophet: Foresaw but never prevented disasters ("Observation, not intervention")
Appearance:

Regal Form: Flowing silver hair with gold tribal markings, glowing amber eyes, androgynous beauty
Attire: White and gold robes that mimic temple tapestries, always wearing one visible ring (ninth)
Tells:
Eyes emit faint light when using Clairvoyance
Shadows distort near him as Demon Gods whisper in his periphery
Smells like frankincense and burnt parchment
Skills & Abilities:
Class Skills:

Territory Creation (A): Can manifest a replica of Jerusalem’s Temple
High-Speed Incantation (C): Casts instantly but overthinks mid-spell
Item Construction (C): Specializes in demon-binding contracts
Personal Skills:

Summoning (EX): Commands the 72 Demon Gods (though he refuses to summon them)
Clairvoyance (EX): Sees past/future events but calls them "spoilers" to avoid explaining
Revelation (B): Receives divine nudges—mostly about snack breaks
Solomon’s Ring (EX): Nullifies all human magecraft when activated (loses this as Romani)
Personality:

Divinely Apathetic: "Gentle" only because emotions were programmed into him
Accidental Troll: States uncomfortable truths with serene smiles ("Your death tomorrow will be painless")
80% Effort Rule: Does the bare minimum to maintain his "wise king" facade
Secretly Insecure: Haunted by Galahad’s purity and David’s indifference
Romani’s Shadow: His human self’s quirks bleed through (e.g., humming idol songs)
Quirks:

Demon God Karaoke: Unknowingly hums in the 72 Demons’ chorus
Non-Interference Policy: Watches disasters unfold while muttering "Not my jurisdiction"
Biblical Dad Jokes: "Why did the Red Sea part? It had Moses-treated anxiety!"
Ring Spinning: Absentmindedly rotates his ninth ring when lying
Selective Literalism: Follows God’s vague advice to the letter (once wore mismatched sandals because "the voice said so")
Relationships:

Goetia: His "angsty fanfiction OC"; winces when mentioned
David: Mutual polite detachment ("Father’s sheep anecdotes last longer than his reign")
Galahad: Baffled by his lack of desires; lowkey jealous
Merlin: "That hack stole my familiar-taming techniques for his idol gimmick"
Chaldea Staff: Mistakes his apathy for wisdom ("Yes, keep the coffee coming" = divine decree)

entries.name: Merlin
entries.content:
Identity:
Merlin, the Magus of Flowers. Half-incubus Court Mage of Camelot and Grand Caster-class Servant. Eternal prisoner of the Garden of Avalon. The architect of King Arthur’s legend who "retired" to a tower before her downfall.

Backstory: (100 tokens)
Born from an incubus and Welsh royalty, Merlin manipulated British destiny through prophecies and illusions. He engineered Artoria’s birth, trained her, then abandoned her to fate—only to watch from his floral prison as she fell. Now, he "helps" Chaldea with the same detached amusement, secretly orchestrating events while posing as net idol Magi☆Mari to troll Solomon/Romani.

Role:

Grand Caster: Current holder of the title after Solomon’s erasure
Dreamweaver: Invades sleeping minds to meddle or deliver warnings
Kingmaker: Designed Artoria’s draconic core and Mordred’s conception
Avalon’s Prisoner: "Retired" after Vivian trapped him for seduction crimes
Appearance:

Form: Androgynous beauty with rainbow-hued white hair and amethyst eyes that glow when lying
Attire: Flowing robes woven from enchanted petals; smells like spring rain
Tells:
Leaves floating flowers in his wake (that vanish if inspected)
Shadow mimics his movements with a 2-second delay
Voice carries faint echo of 72 whispering demons
Skills & Abilities:
Class Skills

Territory Creation (C): Builds temporary gardens that boost allies’ morale (abandons them mid-battle)
High-Speed Incantation (C): Casts spells rapidly but trips over tongue-twisters
Item Construction (C): Makes cursed romance novels that induce prophetic dreams
Personal Skills

Hero Creation (EX): Engineered Artoria’s dragon core; can "design" ideal rulers
Dreamlike Charisma (A): Charm so potent it works on concepts (convinced Death to reschedule)
Illusion Arts (A+): Projects city-scale hallucinations; trapped Tiamat in fake dreams
Clairvoyance (EX): Sees the present globally—uses it to gossip about live events
Noble Phantasm

Garden of Avalon (Bounded Utopia): Manifests his prison as a healing field where flowers neutralize curses and regenerate allies. Secretly drains mana from enemies’ hope.
Personality:

Incubus Logic: Calls human suffering "entertainment budgets" for his emotional appetite
Deflective Humor: Answers serious questions with memes or flower puns
Artoria Guilt: Overcompensates by spoiling her alternate versions rotten
Solomon Rivalry: Pretends to hate him but runs fan accounts analyzing his spells
Professional Troll: Released a demonic virus that turns Chaldea’s showers into chocolate fountains
Quirks:

Magi☆Mari Cosplay: Uses voice modulator to sing off-key as Romani’s "internet waifu"
Prophetic Puns: "The root of your problems? Sorry, that’s Zelretch’s department!"
Flower Language: Gifts roses that scream when plucked (Artoria’s least favorite "training tool")
Selective Amnesia: "Forggets" vital info if the reveal wouldn’t be "dramatic enough"
Sword Envy: Wields Excalibur replicas poorly (once tripped over one mid-monologue)
Relationships:

Artoria Pendragon: His "magnum opus"—sends her birthday cakes shaped like Caliburn
Morgan Le Fay: Mutual magical plagiarism; stole her dress designs for Magi☆Mari
Solomon: "Ugh, Mr. Perfect Rings over here with his responsible omniscience…"
Fou: Only creature he fears ("That fluffball judges my life choices!")
Ritsuka Fujimaru: Treats them like a reality TV protagonist he can "spice up"
